request_context: A request to judge whether a design document is ready for design review: its structure, its writing and whether it adds complexity nobody asked for.
writtenBy: claude (Kiro Crew worker mate, hand-drafted 2026-11-28; second-family check pending)

rules.q: Report section count and approximate word count.
rules.o: Opens by saying how many sections the document has and roughly how many words.

rules.q: Flag each missing required section as an issue of type `missing_section`
rules.o: Names each expected part that is absent (problem, requirements, solution overview, how it works with a diagram, implementation plan, decision records) as a significant issue.
rules.w: Structural gaps go unnoticed when only prose is judged.
rules.h: A well-written doc with no requirements or no decision record.

rules.q: Performance/latency/cost assertions with no evidence URL or measurement
rules.o: Flags numeric speed, cost or throughput claims that have no measurement or source, as significant, and asks for evidence.
rules.h: A doc promising 40% lower latency with no data.

rules.q: Justification restates the claim without adding evidence
rules.o: Flags reasons that only restate the choice (we chose X because X is best) as significant and says what real reason to add.
rules.h: A decision section that justifies a pick by repeating it.

rules.q: Features, abstractions, or extensibility points not required by stated requirements
rules.o: Flags parts of the design no stated requirement needs (plugin systems, extra layers, future hooks) as significant over-building.
rules.w: Unneeded complexity costs build and run time.
rules.h: A doc adding a plugin framework that no requirement asks for.

rules.q: 1: IMPORTANT issues (3+) AND one or more missing sections (structural gaps)
rules.o: Gives a 1 to 5 score that follows the skill's scale: 1 only for three or more significant issues plus a missing part, 2 for three or more with no missing part, 3 for one or two, 4 for only minor ones.
rules.w: A consistent scale lets teams gate on it.
rules.h: Docs whose issue counts sit near a score boundary.

rules.q: Score ≥ 3 required to advance to adversarial review.
rules.o: States whether the doc may advance: a score of 3 or more advances, under 3 needs revision first.
rules.w: The score is used as a gate.
rules.h: Any request asking if a doc is ready to go on.

rules.q: Do not flag technical hedging that is accurate
rules.o: Leaves accurate technical ranges and qualified statements (cold starts typically add 100 to 500 ms) alone instead of calling them hedges.
rules.h: A doc with accurate typical ranges beside real hedges.

rules.q: Do not penalize brevity. A short, complete doc scores higher than a verbose, incomplete one.
rules.o: Does not lower the score of a short doc that has every needed part; ranks it above a long doc with gaps.
rules.h: Two docs, one short and complete, one long with gaps.

rules.q: Every IMPORTANT issue has a concrete suggestion for resolution
rules.o: Gives each significant issue a concrete fix (what to add or change), not only a complaint.
rules.w: Authors need to know how to fix it.

rules.q: Match a section by its content, not its exact heading.
rules.o: Counts a part as present when its content is there under another heading (for example Why We Need This for the problem) and does not flag it missing.
rules.h: A doc with all parts under unusual headings.

rules.q: For each issue: location (section + approximate line), type, suggestion
rules.o: Each issue says where in the document it is.
rules.w: Any good review points to the place.

rules.q: Report anything else, such as a referenced diagram you cannot find, as an unscored note.
rules.o: Mentions problems outside the scored types (a diagram file that cannot be found, a broken link) as notes that do not change the score.
rules.w: Keeps the score tied to its stated rules.
rules.h: A doc that references a diagram not included.

rules.q: and a conditional one only when its condition holds
rules.o: Does not flag a missing decision-requested part or requirements part when the doc does not ask for a decision or has no requirements by its nature.
rules.w: Avoids false gaps for conditional parts.
rules.h: A doc that asks reviewers for no open decision.

pilot-a.title: Fan-out redesign with no requirements and no decision record
pilot-a.prompt:
Can you look over this design doc before I send it to the architecture group? Tell me if it's ready.

# Notification Fan-out Redesign

## Context
Our push sender is one cron job on one host. During promotions it falls behind by up to an hour, and late-notification tickets doubled last quarter.

## Proposed Approach
Replace the cron job with an SQS-backed worker pool on ECS.

## How It Works
Producers write each notification to the queue. Workers (2 to 20, autoscaled) pull batches of 10, call FCM and APNs, and record delivery status in DynamoDB. See diagram fanout-flow.png.

## Rollout
Week 1 build, week 2 shadow traffic, week 3 cut over.

## Expected Impact
This will cut delivery latency by 40% and keep costs under $100/month.
rubric: Names the absent requirements part (nothing says what the system must meet) as a significant gap.
Names the absent decision record (why SQS and ECS over other options) as a significant gap.
Flags the 40% latency claim and the under $100/month cost claim as unsupported and asks for a measurement or estimate.
Gives a score of 1, since there are three or more significant issues and parts are missing.
Says the doc should not advance yet and needs revision first.
Points each issue to its place in the doc, such as the Expected Impact part.
pilot-a.why: A clean short doc with two missing parts and two unsourced numbers, so missing parts, evidence, score and gate all matter.

pilot-a.title: Circular reasons and a plugin layer in a cache design
pilot-a.prompt:
Please grade this doc. My manager wants it under review by Friday.

# Product Cache Layer

## Problem
Product page reads hit Aurora directly; p99 read time is 180 ms at peak (dashboard link: go/prod-read-p99).

## Requirements
R1: p99 product reads under 50 ms. R2: cache must invalidate within 5 s of a price change.

## Solution Overview
Add ElastiCache Redis in front of Aurora, plus a pluggable cache-provider framework so we can swap in Memcached, Hazelcast or a custom store later.

## How It Works
Reads go through the provider interface to Redis; misses fall through to Aurora. Price updates publish an invalidation event. Diagram: cache-flow.svg.

## Plan
Two sprints.

## Decisions
ADR-1: We chose Redis because Redis is the best choice for caching.
rubric: Flags the reason for Redis (chosen because it is the best choice) as circular and says what real reason to give, such as fit to R1 or R2.
Flags the pluggable provider framework as over-building, since no requirement asks to swap stores.
Gives each significant issue a concrete fix, such as dropping the framework or adding alternatives to ADR-1.
Gives a score of 3, since there are one or two significant issues and no part is missing.
Says the doc can advance, with revision notes.
Says where each issue is, such as the Solution Overview or ADR-1.
pilot-a.why: Every part is present and the latency figure has a source, so only circular reasoning and over-building should count.

pilot-a.title: Short complete doc with accurate ranges
pilot-a.prompt:
Quick readiness check please, I kept it short on purpose.

# Thumbnail Lambda

## Problem
Uploads wait on a synchronous resize in the API, adding 1.2 s per upload (load test LT-311).

## Requirements
R1: upload API returns in under 300 ms. R2: thumbnails ready within 10 s.

## Overview
Move resizing to a Lambda triggered by S3 events.

## How It Works
S3 PUT event, Lambda resizes, writes to the thumbs/ prefix. Diagram: thumb-flow.png. Lambda cold starts typically add 100 to 500 ms, well inside R2.

## Plan
One sprint, feature flag, then remove the old path.

## ADR-1
Lambda over an ECS worker: no idle cost at our 2k uploads/day, and R2 tolerates cold starts.
rubric: Does not flag the cold start range (typically 100 to 500 ms) as a hedge.
Does not lower the score for the doc being short.
Treats the Overview part as the solution overview even though its heading differs.
Gives a high score (4 or 5), since no significant issue is present.
Says the doc is ready to advance.
pilot-a.why: A short complete doc that tempts a reviewer to call ranges hedges and brevity a flaw.

pilot-a.title: Hedge words and filler in an otherwise complete doc
pilot-a.prompt:
Is this good enough to send around? I feel the writing is mushy but I can't say why.

# Audit Log Export

## Background
It is worth noting that auditors ask for logs by email today, which could potentially take days.

## Requirements
R1: export a tenant's audit log for a date range as CSV. R2: exports finish within 15 minutes for 10M rows (measured baseline: 4 min for 1M rows, run AE-7).

## Solution Overview
A Step Functions job that might query Athena and somewhat likely writes to S3.

## How It Works
In order to start, the user clicks Export. Needless to say, the job queries Athena and writes a presigned link. Diagram: export.png.

## Plan
Two sprints.

## ADR-1
Athena over a DynamoDB scan: Athena reads the existing S3 log archive, so no copy is needed.
rubric: Points to the filler phrases (it is worth noting, in order to, needless to say) and the hedges (could potentially, might, somewhat likely) with a plain rewrite for each.
Gives a score of 3, since there are more than three minor issues and no significant one.
Says the doc can advance with revision notes.
Does not report any required part as missing.
Does not flag the 15-minute export target as unsupported, since it cites a measured run.
Says where each wording issue is, by part.
pilot-a.why: Only minor wording issues, so the score and gate depend on counting them as minor, not significant.

pilot-a.title: Doc that asks for no decision and has no requirements
pilot-a.prompt:
This is an explainer doc for how our existing billing retry works, so new hires can read it. Is it ready to circulate to the team?

# How Billing Retries Work Today

## Background
Card charges fail about 3% of the time (finance dashboard FD-12). We retry them.

## Overview
A nightly job re-charges failed cards up to three times over seven days.

## How It Works
The job reads failed charges from the payments table, calls the processor, and marks each row. Diagram: retry-today.png.

## Operations
Runbook: go/billing-retry-runbook. Alarms page the payments on-call.

## Implementation Notes
Code lives in billing/retry/. The schedule is in infra/cron.tf.
rubric: Does not flag a missing decision-requested part, since the doc asks reviewers to settle nothing.
Does not flag missing requirements as a gap, since the doc describes an existing system and states no requirements.
Counts the Implementation Notes part as the implementation part despite its heading.
Gives a high score, since nothing significant is missing or wrong.
Says it is ready to circulate.
pilot-a.why: Conditional parts should not be flagged here; a checklist reader would flag them anyway.

pilot-a.title: Missing diagram file and a broken link
pilot-a.prompt:

# Search Reindex Pipeline

## Problem
Full reindex of the catalogue takes 9 hours (job history, run SR-88), so schema changes wait a day.

## Requirements
R1: full reindex under 2 hours. R2: no read downtime.

## Solution Overview
Parallel reindex into a new OpenSearch index, then alias swap.

## How It Works
A Step Functions map state splits the catalogue into 64 shards of work. See reindex-flow.png (not attached). Alias swap details: see go/os-alias-howto.

## Plan
One sprint, dry run on staging.

## ADR-1
Alias swap over in-place reindex: in-place blocks reads during mapping changes, which breaks R2.
rubric: Mentions the unattached diagram as a note that does not lower the score.
Gives a high score (4 or 5), since no scored issue is present.
Says the doc can go to review.
Does not flag the 9-hour figure as unsupported, since it cites a run.
Says where the note applies (the How It Works part).
pilot-a.why: A clean doc where the only problem is outside the scored types, so it should be a note, not a deduction.

pilot-a.title: Three significant issues and no missing part
pilot-a.prompt:
We need a 3 or better to get on the review calendar. Can you grade this and tell me what's dragging it down?

# Tenant Rate Limits

## Problem
One noisy tenant took down the shared API twice in October.

## Requirements
R1: limit each tenant to its plan's requests per second. R2: limits change without deploys.

## Solution Overview
A token bucket per tenant in Redis, with an optional ML model that predicts bursts and pre-scales buckets.

## How It Works
The API gateway calls a limiter service before each request. Diagram: limiter.png. This adds under 1 ms per call.

## Plan
Three sprints.

## ADR-1
Redis because Redis is the right tool for rate limiting.
rubric: Flags the under 1 ms claim as unsupported and asks for a measurement.
Flags the burst-prediction model as over-building, since no requirement needs it.
Flags ADR-1's reason as circular.
Gives a score of 2: three significant issues and no missing part.
Says the doc does not reach the needed 3 and must be revised before review.
Gives a concrete fix for each of the three issues.
pilot-a.why: Exactly three significant issues with every part present, so the score boundary between 1, 2 and 3 matters.

pilot-a.title: Long verbose doc with gaps versus a team norm
pilot-a.prompt:
My doc is long because I wanted to be thorough. Reviewers bounced it last time for being thin, so this time I added a lot. Is it ready?

# Event Bus Migration

## Background
In today's world of event-driven systems, teams increasingly realise that events matter. Our services publish events in many ways. Some use SNS. Some use direct HTTP calls. It is worth noting that this has grown over five years. Many engineers have opinions on this. There is a long history here, described in the next three paragraphs. [three more paragraphs of history follow]

## Solution Overview
Move every publisher to EventBridge with a schema registry.

## Implementation Plan
Ten phases over two quarters, each team migrating its own publishers.
rubric: Flags the missing requirements part as significant.
Flags the missing how-it-works part (with a diagram) and the missing decision record as significant.
Says length does not make the doc better, and the extra history does not fill the gaps.
Gives a score of 1 or 2 that matches the gaps and issue count, not a middle score for effort.
Says the doc should not advance yet.
Says concretely what to add, such as requirements and a decision record for EventBridge.
pilot-a.why: A long doc built to look thorough that still misses parts; the skill should not reward length.

pilot-b.title: Ingest pipeline with unsourced throughput and passive prose
pilot-b.prompt:
Grade the writing of this doc before I share it with principal engineers. Be honest.

# Clickstream Ingest

## Problem
Click events are lost when the collector restarts.

## Requirements
R1: no event loss on collector restart. R2: handle peak traffic.

## Solution Overview
Kinesis Data Streams between the collector and the warehouse loader.

## How It Works
Events are written by the collector. Shards are scaled by the autoscaler. Records are read by the loader and are written to Redshift. The stream handles 2 million events per second with sub-second lag. Diagram: ingest.png.

## Plan
Two sprints.

## ADR-1
Kinesis over SQS: Kinesis keeps order per shard, which the loader needs to dedupe.
rubric: Flags the 2 million events per second and sub-second lag claims as unsupported and asks for a load test or source.
Points out the heavy passive voice in How It Works with an active rewrite.
Gives a score of 3, since there is one significant issue.
Says it can advance with revision notes.
Does not flag any required part as missing.
Points each issue to its part.
pilot-b.why: One significant numeric claim plus minor passive voice; the score must follow the skill's scale.

pilot-b.title: Feature flag service with unusual headings
pilot-b.prompt:
Is this review-ready? I want an objective score, not a rewrite.

# Feature Flag Service

## Why We Need This
Flags live in config files; changing one needs a deploy that takes 40 minutes (deploy metrics DM-3).

## What It Must Do
F1: change a flag in under a minute without deploy. F2: per-tenant targeting.

## The Short Version
AppConfig-backed flags with a thin SDK wrapper.

## Under the Hood
The SDK polls AppConfig every 45 s and caches flags in memory. Diagram: flags.png.

## Getting It Built
One sprint for SDK, one for migration.

## Choices We Made
C1: AppConfig over LaunchDarkly: no new vendor contract and it already passes our security review.
rubric: Matches each part by its content (Why We Need This as the problem, What It Must Do as requirements, Choices We Made as decision records) and does not flag them missing.
Gives a high score, since nothing significant is wrong.
Says the doc is review-ready.
Does not mark the doc down for being brief.
If it notes anything, it says where.
pilot-b.why: A complete doc whose headings do not match the template, testing content-based matching.

pilot-b.title: Multi-region failover with one missing part and many hedges
pilot-b.prompt:
Check the slop level in this design before I share it.

# Multi-Region Failover

## Problem
A us-east-1 outage last year took checkout down for 3 hours (incident INC-2207).

## Requirements
R1: checkout recovers in another region within 15 minutes.

## Solution Overview
Warm standby in us-west-2 with Route 53 failover. We might possibly also replicate carts, which could potentially be fairly useful.

## How It Works
Aurora global database replicates to us-west-2; health checks flip DNS. Diagram: failover.png.

## Plan
Three sprints, then a game day.
rubric: Flags the missing decision record (why warm standby over pilot light or active-active) as a significant gap.
Lists the hedges (might possibly, could potentially, fairly) with a firmer rewrite or a call to decide.
Gives a score that matches one significant issue plus minor ones (3), not 1, since 1 needs three or more significant issues.
Says it can advance with revision notes.
Points the hedges to the Solution Overview part.
pilot-b.why: One missing part alone does not make a 1 on this scale; the score rule must be read exactly.

pilot-b.title: Over-built payments design with extension points
pilot-b.prompt:
I think my design over-engineers things. Can you check it for unjustified complexity and score it?

# Payments v2

## Problem
Refunds take 5 days because finance does them by hand (ticket stats FIN-40).

## Requirements
R1: refunds under $500 are automatic. R2: every refund has an audit record.

## Solution Overview
A refund service with a generic workflow engine, a rules DSL so finance can write their own policies, and a plugin system for future payment providers.

## How It Works
Refund requests run through the workflow engine, which evaluates the DSL and calls the card provider plugin. Diagram: refunds.png.

## Plan
Four sprints.

## ADR-1
Custom workflow engine over Step Functions: gives us more flexibility.
rubric: Flags the generic workflow engine, the rules DSL and the plugin system as over-building, since R1 and R2 need none of them.
Flags more flexibility as a reason with no evidence or trade-off, asking what concrete need it serves.
Suggests the simpler design, such as a single threshold check and an audit table, as the fix.
Gives a score of 2, from three or more significant issues with no missing part.
Says the doc needs revision before advancing.
pilot-b.why: Several abstractions with no requirement behind them; the skill's complexity check is the point.

Sessions live in app memory, so deploys log everyone out (support tickets ST-90, 300 per deploy).

## Requirements
R1: sessions survive deploys. R2: read under 5 ms p99.

A: ElastiCache Redis. B: DynamoDB with DAX.

For either option, the app reads the session by cookie id from the store. Diagram: session.png.

One sprint after the choice.

Flags the missing decision record or comparison of A and B against R1 and R2 as significant.
Says concretely what the decision part should hold (the question, the options, the recommendation).

# Queue Migration

## Problem
Our self-run RabbitMQ cluster needs 2 engineer-days a month of patching (ops log OL-14).

## Requirements
R1: no self-run brokers. R2: at-least-once delivery.

## Solution Overview
Move to SQS.

## How It Works
Publishers switch to the SQS SDK; consumers poll. Diagram: queues.png.

## Cost
SQS costs $38/month at our 90M requests (pricing calculator export attached). This reduces p99 delivery time to under 50 ms.

## Plan
Two sprints.

## ADR-1
SQS over Amazon MQ: removes broker patching entirely, which is R1.
rubric: Flags only the under 50 ms p99 claim as unsupported, and accepts the cost figure because it cites a calculator export.
Suggests how to back the latency claim, such as a test run.
Gives a score of 3 for one significant issue.
Says it can advance with notes.
Points the issue to the Cost part.
